claims.text: An active-learning MLIP trained on ab initio free-energy data can predict solid and liquid free energies.
The proposed MLIP can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The MLIP can attain fidelity comparable to explicit AIMD at a fraction of its computational cost.
The approach can extend from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Training will use targeted ab initio free-energy evaluations selected through active learning.
Free-energy corrections from short, high-accuracy AIMD runs will be incorporated to capture vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects.
The trained MLIP will be deployed in free-energy integration calculations for both solid and liquid phases.
The MLIP will reproduce the ab initio potential-energy surface while embedding free-energy and entropy corrections.
Training on ab initio free-energy and force data will allow the model to learn static configurations and thermal fluctuations.
Efficient MLIP molecular dynamics can be used to perform free-energy integration.
The approach will provide accurate phase free energies at orders-of-magnitude lower cost than full AIMD.
The approach will be more efficient than TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
Phase free energies, melting temperatures, and entropy changes will agree with explicit AIMD results to within approximately 5–10%.
The method will reduce computation time by approximately 10- to 100-fold relative to AIMD.
The method will offer greater throughput than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The intended composition domain runs from pure elements and simple binaries through moderately complex high-entropy alloys.
The intended temperature domain is near the melting point, where vibrational and anharmonic effects remain significant.
Performance may vary with system complexity, and incomplete training coverage of entropy contributions may cause inaccuracies in highly complex multicomponent systems.
A benchmark against AIMD, plus TOR-TILD for a binary system, will compare phase free-energy differences, melting temperature, transition entropy, latent heat, and computational time.
The hypothesis is falsified by errors above approximately 10% in the specified thermodynamic predictions or by a speedup below 10-fold relative to AIMD.
